title: An Interview with Mei Tan
subject: Mei Tan
text:
TITLE: An Interview with Mei Tan
SUBJECT: Mei Tan, born Mei Chen, friend and former business partner of Nora Bennett
INTERVIEWER: Helen Ward
DATE OF INTERVIEW: 2026-03-02
NOTE: This is fictional training data for the Memoirs demo. All names, places and events are invented.

[00:00:11] HELEN: Could you tell me where your story begins?

[00:00:19] MEI: Penang, though I was born in Ipoh in 1953. My parents moved when I was small because my father found work at a printing company. At school I was Mei Chen. After I married Raymond Tan in 1976, I became Mei Tan. I kept Chen on some documents because changing every record was exhausting. In Australia most people know me as Mei Tan, and some old friends still call me Mei Chen.

[00:01:21] MEI: I came to Adelaide in 1974 as a student. The plan was to study accounting for two years and return home. Plans are polite suggestions made by people who have not yet met their future. I found work in a bookkeeping office, then married Raymond. We separated in the late eighties and never made a dramatic announcement about it. We simply stopped sharing a house.

[00:02:18] HELEN: How did you meet Nora?

[00:02:25] MEI: It was not an English class. Nora remembers an English class because she was always attending one. We met at a community cooking course in 1989, where she burned the onions and blamed the saucepan. I had been in Australia for fifteen years by then, so I was the one explaining local forms and school notices. She had recently arrived and was trying to understand everything at once.

[00:03:19] MEI: Her full name is Nora Bennett, but her sisters call her Norrie. Priya calls her Mum, and the grandchildren call her Nana Norrie. When I first knew her she introduced herself as Nor, which I thought was a nickname for Eleanor. We laughed about that for years.

[00:04:02] HELEN: When did you decide to open the cafe?

[00:04:08] MEI: The idea began in 1991, but The Lantern opened in March 1992. Nora sometimes says 1991 because we signed the lease that year. The distinction mattered to me because I kept the accounts. We had a small shop on Grange Road, between a shoe repairer and a place that sold picture frames.

[00:05:05] MEI: Nora was the public face. She remembered birthdays, school concerts and who was waiting for a doctor's appointment. I did the purchasing and most of the cooking. We disagreed about coriander, music and whether a customer who had not paid for three months was still a customer. We never disagreed about closing time. We were both tired by nine.

[00:06:02] MEI: The cafe was not successful in the way people mean successful. We did not become rich. But it paid the rent and created a room where strangers could become familiar. In 1994, an elderly man named Walter started coming every Tuesday with a notebook. He was writing letters to his grandchildren and asked Nora to check his spelling. By 1997 he was reading the letters aloud to anyone who would listen.

[00:07:01] HELEN: Do you remember anything difficult?

[00:07:07] MEI: In the winter of 1996, a woman named Evelyn left a red suitcase outside. Nora says it happened in October, but I remember July because we were serving pumpkin soup. The suitcase had family photographs and letters. We put a notice in the window and asked the bus company. It came back after two days. I do not know whether Evelyn was more relieved to find the suitcase or to find that strangers had cared.

[00:08:04] MEI: Nora's husband Alan became ill around 2001. I should say he was ill before then, but that was when the illness changed what the family could manage. My mother also needed help. The Lantern closed in 2003, not because of one event but because too many responsibilities arrived at once.

[00:08:53] MEI: After the closure, Nora returned to the school library. She started an oral-history group in 2005, perhaps 2006. I remember attending the first meeting and bringing a folder of old cafe menus. She said the menus were evidence that ordinary people had been there. I thought she was being sentimental. Later I understood that sentiment is sometimes another word for information we do not want to lose.

[00:09:42] HELEN: What should a memoir preserve?

[00:09:48] MEI: It should preserve the uncertainty as well as the dates. People remember the meaning of an event before they remember the calendar. If three people tell you that The Lantern opened in three different years, that is not only a problem to correct. It tells you which part of the event stayed alive for each person. The record should show the disagreement and the evidence, not choose a neat answer just because a database prefers one.

[00:10:22] MEI: And it should remember the small things. The leaking refrigerator. Walter's blue notebook. Nora keeping sugar packets in a drawer for children who were too shy to ask. Those details are not decoration. They are how a life becomes recognizable.
